newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: New Zealand in suspense after tight election.
newsitem.headline: New Zealand in suspense after tight election.

text.p: New Zealand plunged into political uncertainty on Sunday with no clear coalition in sight after voters delivered a split verdict on six years of conservative rule.

Prime Minister Jim Bolger said he would try to form a new minority government, but opposition Labour leader Helen Clark sought coalition talks with nationalist New Zealand First and the left-wing Alliance.
"I know that many people have expressed the hope that I will break through that glass ceiling and be the first woman prime minister of New Zealand," Clark told cheering supporters.
"I will be endeavouring to negotiate to see that I can lead a change of government, and certainly leadership of this country is something that I would consider a great honour to accept."
But Bolger, who has a potential partner in radical free-market Act New Zealand, was optimistic of holding onto power. He urged financial markets to keep calm.

"We know that New Zealand will be able to form a sensible government, a forward-looking government, a government that you and I would be prepared to be part of as we move forward through the next three years," he told followers of his National Party.
The balance of power lay with New Zealand First, which wants to cut immigration and limit foreign stakes in "strategic" assets to less than 25 percent.

Its charismatic Maori leader, Winston Peters, has refused to say which of National and Labour he would favour as coalition partner. "We'll be seeking political and economic stability, the best interests of our country, real solutions to the outstanding social problems that bedevil us," he declared.
All sides agreed that Peters's role was pivotal. "Where Peters goes, I guess, goes government," said government spokesman Richard Griffin.

With 97 percent of the vote counted, television projections gave National 44 seats, Labour 37, NZ First 17, the Alliance 13 and Act eight in the new 120-member parliament. The small centrist United Party, expected to favour National, won one.
The murky outcome of New Zealand's first election under German-style proportional representation promised weeks, perhaps months, of tough coalition negotiations.
National campaigned on its record of economic growth, budget surpluses and tax cuts, but lost ground as rivals attacked its record on health, education and social policy.
Labour ran a strong campaign based on pledges to share more widely the benefits of 12 years of free-market reform, which many see as having widened the gap between rich and poor.
The left-wing Alliance, which wants big increases in taxes and government spending, has ruled out joining a formal coalition but signalled it may support Labour on key issues.
Financial markets favour National but analysts say they would be comfortable with a Labour-led coalition, provided the Alliance plays a limited role.

The Alliance and New Zealand First both oppose asset sales and want to buy back Forestry Corporation, sold recently by the government to a consortium of local companies and China's Citic for NZ$2 billion (US$1.39 billion). ($1 = $NZ$1.44)
